content: Ringworm, also referred to as Tinea, is a fungal infection of the skin. It is characterized by a reddish to brownish raised or bumpy patch of skin that often appears lighter in the center, creating a ring-like appearance. Despite its name, ringworm is not caused by a worm but by parasitic fungi, specifically dermatophytes. These fungi feed on keratin, a protein found in the outer layer of the skin, hair, and nails. They thrive in warm, moist, and dark environments. Dermatophyte infections, including ringworm, are common, affecting up to 20% of the population at any given time. Ringworm is highly contagious and can spread through direct skin-to-skin contact or by coming into contact with contaminated objects such as hairbrushes or shared toilet seats. Individuals involved in contact sports, such as wrestling, are at increased risk due to frequent skin-to-skin contact. Ringworm can also be transmitted from animals, particularly domestic pets like cats and dogs, as well as farm animals. Humans can contract the infection through close contact with these animals. Additionally, prolonged exposure to shed skin flakes, such as from shared clothing or household dust, can lead to infection. Certain individuals, such as those with eczema or other skin conditions, are more susceptible due to a compromised skin barrier. Children are particularly vulnerable before puberty, and some people may have a genetic predisposition to recurrent infections. The hallmark symptom of ringworm in humans is the presence of one or more red, raised, itchy patches with well-defined edges. These patches often have a lighter center, resembling a ring. When the scalp or beard area is affected, bald patches may develop. The infected area may itch intermittently. Diagnosis is typically made based on clinical appearance, but a physician may also take a skin scraping or examine plucked hairs under a microscope to identify fungal elements. In some cases, samples are cultured on specialized agar plates in a microbiology lab. Certain fungi fluoresce under black light, aiding in diagnosis. In animals, symptoms may include scaling and hair loss, though some cats can be asymptomatic carriers. Occasionally, a ringworm infection may trigger skin lesions in distant areas of the body, known as dermatophytids, which are allergic reactions to the fungus. These lesions are fungus-free and usually resolve once the primary infection is treated. Treatment for ringworm typically involves topical antifungal medications, such as miconazole, clotrimazole, terbinafine, butenafine, or tolnaftate, many of which are available over the counter. For scalp infections, shampoos containing pyrithione zinc, such as Head and Shoulders, can be effective. Terbinafine has been approved for use in children aged four and older and is available in granule form for easy administration. In cases of severe itching, burning, or scaling, antifungal ointments may be combined with hydrocortisone creams to reduce inflammation and promote healing. However, infections involving the nails or scalp can be particularly challenging to treat due to the fungus residing in follicle roots or beneath the nail. Oral antifungal medications, such as griseofulvin, are often required for these cases. In animals, treatments may include sulfurated lime rinses, diluted povidone-iodine washes, or enilconazole rinses. Lufenuron, commonly used as an oral flea treatment, is also prescribed for ringworm in cats and dogs. Folk remedies for ringworm often involve the use of caustic or acidic substances, herbal poultices, or oils like tea tree oil. However, the efficacy of these treatments is unproven, and some may cause more harm than the fungal infection itself. Preventing ringworm involves maintaining good hygiene and avoiding shared personal items such as clothing, towels, or sports equipment. After participating in sports involving skin-to-skin contact, individuals should shower and shampoo thoroughly. Wrestlers should inspect their skin regularly, use protective bandages over infections, and disinfect gym equipment. Wearing loose-fitting cotton clothing and keeping the skin clean and dry are also important preventive measures. Pets with patches of missing hair should be evaluated by a veterinarian, as this may indicate a fungal infection. Topical treatments should be continued for 2 to 4 weeks after symptoms resolve to ensure complete eradication of the fungus.
